chunks: Mu'ammarr ibn Khalld narrated from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I was sitting with him on the last day of Sha'ban. I did not see him fasting, so they brought him a meal, and he said, 'Come near.' This was after the Asr prayer. I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, I fasted today.' He said to me, 'Why?' I said, 'It has been narrated from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding the day of doubt that he said, 'A day that Allah made successful (Yawm Waffaqallahu Lah).' He said, 'Do you not know that this is only if it is not known whether it is from Sha'ban or from the month of Ramadan? If the man fasted it and it turned out to be from the month of Ramadan, it was a day that Allah made successful. But if there is no reason (illat) and no doubt, then no.' I said, 'I will break my fast now.' He said, 'No.' I said, 'And so is it with the voluntary fasts? Is it not permissible for me to break my fast after Dhuhr?' He said, 'Yes.'

key_terms.رَمَضَان: Ramadan, the ninth month of fasting
key_terms.شَعْبَان: Sha'ban, the eighth month of the Islamic lunar calendar
key_terms.يَوْمُ الشُّبْهَةِ: The day of doubt, referring to the 30th of Sha'ban when it is uncertain if it is the last day of Sha'ban or the first of Ramadan

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting the day of doubt in Sha'ban and can one break a voluntary fast after Dhuhr?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between fasting the 'day of doubt' (Shakk) as a precautionary measure versus fasting it when it is definitively known to be Sha'ban. The Imam emphasizes that while fasting on the day of doubt is rewarded as if it were Ramadan, it lacks the specific legal weight of an obligatory fast if no genuine uncertainty exists, yet voluntary fasting remains permissible even after Dhuhr. This reflects the Shia scholarly principle of distinguishing between the certainty of obligation and the merit of voluntary worship during transitional lunar months.
